newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan orders repair of riot-damaged churches.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan orders repair of riot-damaged churches.

text.p: Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on Thursday ordered urgent repairs at state expense of churches recently damaged by Moslem rioters in the central province of Punjab, a government source said.

He said Sharif had also told authorities to pay generous compensation for losses suffered by the Christian villagers near the southern Punjab town of Khanewal in the February attack by thousands of protesters.

Sharif asked the interior ministry and the Punjab provincial government to arrest people responsible for the attack, in which at least two people were killed by police firing and 19 others were injured.
In speeches after taking office last week, Sharif has been assuring protection for Christians and other minority communities and promising punishment for the attackers.
Thousands of enraged Moslems had rampaged through villages of Christians Khanewal, accusing them of blasphemy against Islam, a charge denied by the Christians.

Moslems accused some Christians of throwing torn pages of the Koran into mosques and thus committing blasphemy, which carries the death penatly in Pakistan. The Christians denied the allegation and said the local police officials might have thrown the pages into mosques to provoke the attacks to avenge an earlier Christian protest against the police.
Christian residents accused the attackers of burning their homes and churches and assaulting women.
Most of Pakistan's 131 million people are Moslems, but there is a small Christian minority, some of whose members have been accused by radical Moslem clerics of blasphemy in recent years.
In February 1995, two Christians, one of them a 14-year-old boy, were sentenced to death for blasphemy in the Punjab capital Lahore, but were acquitted on an appeal and then emigrated to Germany.

Then-prime minster Benazir Bhutto vowed at the time to alter the blasphemy law to make it less open to abuse complained by Christians and human rights groups, but pressure from religious parties blocked any change.
